Today they refine the voice of that draft.","enduringUnderstanding":"Strong explanatory writers choose a formal, consistent voice and connect ideas with transitions so readers can follow how stories share values and lessons.","futureLessons":"In Lesson 39, students will revise for capitalization, punctuation and spelling and peer-review one another's essays. Today's work on formal style, transitions and conclusions builds the cohesion and tone of the final essay."},"vocabulary":[{"word":"formal style","definition":"A way of writing that uses complete sentences, precise words and no slang, contractions or casual phrases.","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"tone","definition":"The attitude a writer shows toward a topic, created through word choice.","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"consistent","definition":"Staying the same throughout, without unexpected changes.","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"transition","definition":"A word or phrase that shows how ideas, sentences or paragraphs connect.","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"cohesive","definition":"Holding together so that ideas connect and flow logically.","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"verb tense","definition":"The form of a verb that shows when an action happens: past, present or future.","tier":"support"},{"word":"conclusion","definition":"The final section of an essay that follows from the explanation and leaves the reader with a final thought.","tier":"support"}],"texts":[{"title":"The Lightning Thief","author":"Rick Riordan","pages":"Students' chosen passages for their essay evidence"},{"title":"Example explanatory essay (teacher model)","pages":"Full text"}]},"sections":[{"kind":"launch","title":"Launch","purpose":"Reconnect students to the performance task and set a focus on sounding formal and consistent as they keep drafting.","activities":[{"id":"launch-formal-or-casual","title":"Formal or Casual?","minutes":5,"standards":["L.6.3.b","W.6.2.e"],"routine":"Turn and Talk","blocks":[{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"Display two versions of one sentence about the novel. Casual: Percy is like, super brave when he goes after Medusa, and it's kinda a big deal. Formal: Percy shows courage when he confronts Medusa, and this moment reveals his growing confidence."},{"type":"directions","text":"Read both sentences. With a partner, decide which one belongs in our essays and name two words or phrases that helped you decide."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which sentence sounds right for an essay, and what clues told you?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The second one. The first has 'like,' 'super' and 'kinda,' which sound like talking to a friend. The second uses 'shows courage' and 'reveals,' which sound more serious and exact."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Today you keep drafting your Shared Stories, Shared Lessons essay. Your goal is a voice that stays formal from the first sentence to the last, with transitions that connect your ideas."}]}]},{"kind":"literacy-lab","title":"Literacy Lab","purpose":"Mini-lesson on consistent verb tense and transition phrases that signal comparison and classification across paragraphs.","activities":[{"id":"lab-tense-and-transitions","title":"Tense Check and Transition Phrases","minutes":10,"standards":["L.6.3","L.6.3.b","W.6.2.c"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"When we write about literature, we usually use present tense: Percy discovers, Riordan writes. If we slip into past tense halfway through, the style feels inconsistent. Transitions also matter. To compare, use similarly, likewise, in contrast, however. To classify, use one type, another category, for example, in addition."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Model paragraph: Percy learned he was a demigod. He faces monsters at camp. In contrast, Perseus fights Medusa alone. Another kind of challenge, for example, is choosing loyalty over safety."},{"type":"directions","text":"Read the model paragraph. Underline each verb and circle any that shift tense. Rewrite the sentence in present tense. Then box each transition and write whether it compares or classifies."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which verb breaks the pattern, and how do you fix it?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"'Learned' is past tense and the others are present. I would change it to 'learns' so the whole paragraph stays in present tense."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which transitions signal comparison, and which signal classification?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"'In contrast' compares Percy and Perseus. 'Another kind' and 'for example' sort the challenges into types."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Keep this to about 10 minutes. Students will apply the skill to their own drafts in Learning in Action, so do not over-practice here."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: Spotting tense shifts","tryThis":"Have students read aloud only the verbs in order, listening for the one that sounds different. Provide a sentence frame: In my essay, I write about the book in ___ tense."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to find a transition in their own draft that is overused (such as 'also') and replace it with a more precise comparison or classification phrase."}]}]}]},{"kind":"learning-in-action","title":"Learning in Action","purpose":"Model formal style with an example essay, then students continue drafting body paragraphs with evidence, transitions and a concluding section.","activities":[{"id":"lia-model-formal-style","title":"Model: Consistent Formal Style and Tone","minutes":8,"standards":["L.6.3.b","W.6.2.e","W.6.2.d","W.6.4"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"Example explanatory essay (teacher model)","pages":"Body paragraph 2 and conclusion"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"I am rereading my body paragraph the way a reader would. I highlight informal words in yellow, such as 'a lot' or 'kind of.' Then I swap them for precise words. 'A lot of courage' becomes 'remarkable courage.' I also check that the tone stays serious and respectful the whole way through."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What did the writer change to keep the tone consistent, and why does it matter?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The writer replaced casual phrases with exact words and avoided contractions. It matters because if the tone changes, the reader may stop trusting the explanation."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Now the conclusion. A strong ending does not add a new topic. It follows from what the essay explained and says what the lessons from both stories mean."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does this conclusion follow from the information in the essay?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"It restates the shared lesson about loyalty from both stories and explains why the lesson matters, so it connects back to the thesis instead of starting something new."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Students notice the difference between informal and formal language and begin using more precise words and detail-adding phrases.","sayAsk":"Say: Let's change 'a lot' to a precise word. Ask: What is a more formal way to say 'kind of scary'? Frames: Instead of ___, I can write ___. The writer shows a formal tone by ___. Add detail with adverbials: Percy acts bravely during the battle. Percy hesitates before he speaks.","watchFor":"If students copy informal speech into writing, then have them say the idea aloud in a school voice first and write that version. If students add details only with adjectives, then prompt for how, when or where. Success: student replaces at least two informal phrases with precise formal language."}]},{"id":"lia-draft-essay","title":"Draft and Strengthen the Essay","minutes":17,"standards":["W.6.2","W.6.2.a","W.6.2.b","W.6.2.c","W.6.2.e","W.6.2.f","W.6.9","W.6.10","L.6.3.b"],"routine":"Independent Writing","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Continue drafting your essay. (1) Finish or strengthen at least two body paragraphs, each with relevant evidence from The Lightning Thief and your second source that supports your thesis, plus your own explanation. (2) Use transitions that signal comparison or classification to connect your paragraphs. (3) Keep your verbs in present tense and your tone formal. (4) Draft your concluding section so it follows from your explanation. If you are typing, use your keyboarding time to produce as much of the draft as you can."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Circulate and confer with 4 to 5 students. Look for evidence that is quoted but not explained, paragraphs that start abruptly with no transition, and slang or contractions. Use the prompts in the ELD panel and support table."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"(During conferences) How does this evidence prove your thesis, and what transition will lead your reader into the next idea?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"This quote shows Percy choosing to protect his friend, which proves my thesis about loyalty. I will start my next paragraph with 'In contrast' because the myth hero acts alone."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["W.6.2.f"],"stem":"A student's essay explains how both The Lightning Thief and a Greek myth teach lessons about loyalty. Which concluding sentence best follows from that explanation?","choices":[{"text":"Both stories show that loyalty to others can matter more than personal glory, a lesson that remains meaningful today.","correct":true,"rationale":"It follows from the explanation and ties the shared lesson back to the thesis."},{"text":"Greek gods are very powerful, and Poseidon is the god of the sea.","correct":false,"rationale":"This introduces new facts unrelated to the essay's explanation of loyalty."},{"text":"Anyway, that's all I have to say about the books.","correct":false,"rationale":"It uses an informal tone and does not draw a conclusion from the explanation."},{"text":"Percy is my favorite character because he is funny.","correct":false,"rationale":"It states a personal opinion that does not follow from the explanatory information."}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Students draft with transitions and added details, expanding sentences to explain how, when or why.","sayAsk":"Say: Use a transition to link your ideas. Ask: What word shows how this paragraph connects to the last one? Frames: Similarly, ___. In contrast, ___. One type of ___ is ___. This evidence shows that ___ because ___. Expand: Percy chooses to stay ___ (where) because ___ (why).","watchFor":"If students list evidence with no explanation, then prompt: 'What does this show about the lesson?' If students use only 'and' or 'also,' then offer the comparison and classification word bank. Success: student uses at least two transitions and explains each piece of evidence."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: Connecting evidence to the thesis","tryThis":"Provide the frame: This evidence shows ___, which supports my thesis that ___. Let students say the explanation aloud to a partner before writing."},{"situation":"Struggling with: Starting a conclusion","tryThis":"Offer: Both stories teach that ___. This matters because ___. Have students reread their thesis first."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to add an abstract noun (such as loyalty, courage or sacrifice) to the conclusion and define it in the context of both stories."}]}]},{"id":"lia-highlight-cohesion","title":"Highlight Cohesive Devices","minutes":5,"standards":["W.6.2.c","W.6.4","L.6.3.b"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Reread your draft. Highlight every transition in one color. Underline any verb that changes tense. Circle any informal word. Fix at least three items."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What did the highlighting show you about how your essay connects?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"I saw that my second paragraph had no transition at all. I added 'In contrast' at the beginning. I also fixed two verbs that were in past tense."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Students check their writing for cohesion and detail with a visual tool and sentence frames.","sayAsk":"Say: Show me one transition you highlighted. Frames: I highlighted ___ to connect ___. I changed ___ to ___ so the tense stays the same.","watchFor":"If students highlight nothing, then point to the start of each paragraph and ask how it links to the one before. I still need to finish my conclusion and add evidence to my last body paragraph."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Optional starter: Today I improved my essay by ___.
